author: Reichsarchiv
title: Der Weltkrieg 1914 bis 1918. Die militärischen Operationen zu Lande, Band 1: Die Grenzschlachten im Westen
notes: German official history; volumes 1, 3 and 4 cover the West in 1914. Authoritative for German orders of battle, daily positions and orders; apologetic in tone on command decisions, and it measures the campaign by what the German army did — the Belgian and French sides appear only as resistance met. Band 1, pp. 105–120 ('Die Eroberung der Festung Lüttich') is the account of the Liège operation and the reduction of the twelve forts, and is this pack's citation for when each of them fell: it gives the day and the part of the day — an afternoon, a forenoon, an evening — and not the clock. Page references are to the 1925 first edition, digitised at the URL above. Where a fort-by-fort record at clock resolution is wanted, the works to bring in are Donnell and Zuber (docs/sources.md, 'To add as the content lands'). Beyond the forts, this pack cites it with pages for Emmich's order to advance on Liège 'am 4. August früh' and the composition of the Army of the Meuse (p. 109); the 54th Brigade stepping off from Hermée at 2.30 a.m. on 6 August, the one hour the assault account prints (p. 112); Leman's order sending the 3rd Division away, the movement begun in the afternoon of the 6th, and the garrison of the fortress as about 50,000 men against the 6,000 the Germans assumed (p. 117); the marches of 20 August on the line Brussels–Droogenbosch–Waterloo and the III Reserve Corps taking over the screen against Antwerp (pp. 219, 222); and Gallwitz's report that the northern forts of Namur had fallen (p. 395). For the order of battle it is Anlage 1, 'Das deutsche Westheer am 18. August 1914, beim Beginn des Vormarsches' (pp. 664–687), that this pack cites: it prints every army with its battalion, squadron, battery and gun totals, and under each army every corps with its commander, its chief of staff and its two divisions. pp. 69–70 give what came before it — the deployment areas the Aufmarschanweisungen laid down for each of the seven armies and the four cavalry corps, and the Nordarmee in Schleswig-Holstein; p. 71 records that the transfer of the IX. Armeekorps from the 2. to the 1. Armee was foreseen from the start, which is why the deployment list on p. 69 and the order of battle on pp. 667–668 put that corps in different armies. pp. 688–691 carry the same treatment of the French army, which this pack uses to arbitrate where Edmonds's Appendix 3 and the content disagree. For the routes (sand-23b.6.2) it was read again for its dated situation sketches, which are printed in the text and not in the map pocket: Skizze 2 (p. 195), the 6th and 7th Armies on the morning of 14 August; Skizze 3 (p. 347) and Skizze 7 (p. 506), the 1st, 2nd and 3rd Armies on the mornings of 21 and 25 August; Skizze 8 (p. 538), the 4th and 5th Armies on the morning of 24 August. The narrative behind them: pp. 214–225 the advance of the wheeling wing 18–20 August (20 August 'ein reiner Marschtag', the 1st Army's objectives on the line Brüssel–Droogenbosch–Waterloo and every corps' halting place, the 2nd Army on Mont-St. Jean–La Gatte, the 3rd on Spontin–Celles–Ciergnon); pp. 263–302 the battle in Lorraine corps by corps; pp. 348–430 the Sambre, Namur and Mons; pp. 505–535 the pursuit to 27 August, with the 2nd Army's positions on the evening of the 25th and its objectives for the 26th at pp. 508–509; pp. 537–567 the centre; pp. 568–603 the left wing. **The volume's narrative stops on 27 August** — nothing after that date can be cited to it, which is why the Guise routes were re-pointed to Bd. 3 and the Marne routes keep no pages.
